form: Abstract: ’Wuikala is a stress language, placing stress on the heaviest leftmost moraic syllable within a prosodic word. The phonemic system displays contrastive vowel and resonant length, which are considered heavy, or bi-moraic syllables. The leftmost heavy syllable will always surface with stress. If there are no heavy syllables, the leftmost moraic syllable will host stress. ’Wuikala does not show lexically stressed suffixes, as in Haisla, or lexical tone, as in Heiltsuk-Xai’xais. If there are no moraic syllables within a word, no syllable surfaces with stress.

form: ’Wuikala (ISO 639-3 wui) is the most under-researched language within the North Wakashan language family. It has historically been categorized as Northern Kwakiutl (Boas 1911), or as Heiltsuk (Eberhard et al. 2025, in Ethnologue; Yinka Déné Language Institute 2006), both of which are neighbouring and related languages, but distinct in all important respects, including communal identity, and are all properly considered as separate languages (Hilton & Rath 1982:7). One of these linguistic distinctions is the prosodic system, in which ’Wuikala differs from its neighbours, by not being tonal as Heiltsuk is (Kortlandt 1978), but showing a more complex prosodic system than Kwak̓wala (Bach 1975, Janzen 2015).

form: This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides some background on moraicity as the basis of the stress system in ’Wuikala. Section 3 investigates the stress system of ’Wuikala, using examples of language data to show that standard North Wakashan Stress (SNWS) applies, is disrupted by long vowels and long resonants, does not have a default-to-opposite system like Kwak̓wala or Haisla, or lexically tonal suffixes like Haisla or Heiltsuk-Xai’xais. Section 4 concludes.

form: ’Wuikala stress has been reported to conform to what I refer to as Standard North Wakashan Stress (SNWS), stating that word stress falls broadly on the first vocalic plain resonant (Hilton & Rath 1982:22, Nater 1987:4). However, until now this claim has never been investigated fully. The most detailed research into ’Wuikala was conducted by Flynn (Howe 2000a), which is a study on segmental phonology of the language and has little to say directly about the prosodic system of ’Wuikala. Nevertheless, this resource is primary for my understanding of ’Wuikala phonology, along with available audio content from the ’Wuikala First Voices page, and text data from the local dictionary (‘Wuìkinux̌v Language Department 2004).

form: The sister languages within the Upper North Wakashan group, Heiltsuk-Xai’xais and Haisla, both display levels of lexical stress. Heiltsuk-Xai’xais is a tonal system (Kortlandt 1975), with many morphemes displaying associated lexical tone, as well as a SNWS system (Janzen 2025). Haisla has a limited number of suffixes displaying lexical stress, which disrupt an otherwise predictable SNWS system (Lincoln & Rath 1986, Howe 2005, Janzen 2023). In the next section, I show that these prosodic traits do not exist in ’Wuikala.

form: A significant departure from Flynn’s phonemic inventory in Howe (2000a:21) in the inclusion of the long mid vowels [ɛː, ɔː] and the removal of the so-called glottalized vowels i̓, u̓, a̓. I treat the latter as schwa glottal pairings: əy̓, əw̓, əʔ respectively. These would not be considered moraic. Moraic segments are full vowels [i, u, a] and schwa non-glottalized-resonant pairings within the same syllable [əl., ən., əm.], including the long resonants [mː, nː, lː] which I assume to be syllabic. Notably for the stress system, long vowels and resonants are considered bi-moraic and attract stress over other non-heavy syllables.

form: Word stress is defined here as an increase in pitch, duration, and intensity of one syllable nucleus over all other syllables within the prosodic word. Stress in the community orthography is marked with a grave accent “ ` ”, and should appear on all multisyllabic words. Long vowels and resonants are marked orthographically with a doubling of the segment and the grave accent on the second of the repeated segments (e.g. iì, uù, aù, aì). This serves to unify the long segment as one phonological unit (aù [ɔ́ː]). However, the application of the stress mark in ’Wuikala is inconsistent throughout the various learning resources available. I have mitigated these inconsistencies as best I could by relying on those audio resources available on the ’Wuikala First Voices page. I have only included examples that I could independently verify the stress placement of, through the audio given from this website, unless otherwise noted.

form: As stated, what I describe as standard North Wakashan stress largely accounts for the stress placement in ’Wuikala. This is as far as the literature goes into investigating this system, most concisely put here:

form: “In [’Wuikala], the first vocalic plain resonant of the word automatically bears stress when it is not followed by another vocalic plain resonant... When the first plain resonant of a word is immediately followed by a second, the stress falls on the latter... However, phonetically, the second resonant need not necessarily be pronounced with noticeably greater loudness than the first. As long as its phonetic actualization is not less loud than that of the first, the stress is phonologically on the second.”

form: Lincoln & Rath are essentially stating that SNWS is the default, with the exception of an initial vowel series. Lincoln & Rath use the term ‘resonant’ to refer to both consonants and vowels, but I use the term here only for consonants [n, m, l]. They give the examples dəná ‘pull’, dənə́m ‘buoy line’, ciá ‘get water’. In each case, there is a seemingly moraic segment after an onset consonant, with an immediately following equally moraic segment a, em, a respectively. Following the approach by Inman & Werle (2025), I describe the relative moraicity of adjacent vowels as a repair strategy in Upper North Wakashan languages. All syllables in every North Wakashan language must have an onset. Stated simply, when a moraic segment appears following another moraic segment, the first is reduced to a schwa-resonant pair (u → əw), in effect, removing its moraic projection to provide an onset to the following vowel through syllabification /Cə.wV́/. The adjoining vowel then often becomes the leftmost moraic segment in the word and receives stress.

form: In this example sentence, two words have reduced vowels, the second of which has an impact on word stress. The first is the alternation between w̓ác̓i ‘dog’ and w̓ác̓əyaꭓi ‘the dog there’, where the [i] vowel is reduced to [əy] when followed by the deictic clitic [aꭓi]. The stress therefore falls on the leftmost moraic segment of the word, which is [ə́m] ləʔə́mnƛənƛənc ‘down to us’.

form: Like sister language Haisla, ’Wuikala has contrastive vowel length. Unlike Haisla, ’Wuikala also shows contrastive resonant length: (e.g. y̕ak̓ ‘bad’ vs. t̓aːx ‘gun powder’; ƛ̓mq̓ ‘yew tree’ vs. smːs ‘mouth’) (Howe 2000a:5). I describe these long segments as bi-moraic, meaning they have two morae and are therefore prosodically heavy. The local orthography often confuses the distribution of long vowels by spelling out predictable high vowel lowering (Howe 2000a:153) following non-rounded uvulars, i.e. gàx̌ax̌ailh [gáꭓaꭓiɬ] “coming down inside”. These are orthographically identical to long vowels, but are not, in fact, phonologically long. When finding examples I carefully avoided instances of orthographic ‘ai’ or ‘au’ sequences when following any uvular phoneme.

form: This paper has investigated the stress system of ’Wuikala, showing that Standard North Wakashan Stress (SNWS) is the primary mechanism governing stress assignment: the leftmost moraic syllable within the prosodic word bears stress. Moraicity in ’Wuikala is determined by full vowels [i, u, a] and schwa-resonant pairings [əl., ən., əm.] within the same syllable. Schwa alone, and schwa-glottalized resonant pairings (əl̓, əm̓, ən̓), are non-moraic and are ignored in stress assignment. A small set of words contain no moraic material whatsoever and surface as stressless.

form: I identify two disruptions to SNWS. First, long vowels and long resonants are bi-moraic and prosodically heavy. They attract stress even when they are not the leftmost moraic element in the word. Second, when two moraic segments are adjacent, a syllable repair strategy reduces the first to a schwa-resonant pair, effectively removing its moraic projection and allowing the following segment to host stress.

form: Crucially, ’Wuikala patterns differently from its Upper North Wakashan sister language in two respects. Unlike Heiltsuk-Xai'xais, it does not employ lexical tone. Unlike Haisla, it has no lexically stressed suffixes capable of disrupting predictable SNWS assignment. The cognate suffixes shared with Haisla surface in ’Wuikala with stress determined entirely by the moraicity and syllable structure of the stem, not by any lexical property of the suffix itself. ’Wuikala's stress system is, therefore, fully predictable from prosodic structure alone.
